tasks.q: Write a program that reports the length of a word and the characters at each end of it.
brief: Read one word.
Print how many characters it has on the first line.
Print its first character on the second line.
Print its last character on the third line.
tasks.starter: # Read a word, then print its length, its first character and its last character

tests.why: bridge has 6 characters. The first character is at position 0, so w[1] would give you r instead of b.
With one character the first and the last are the same one. A crash here means you used a fixed position such as w[5] rather than working from the length.
The last character is w[-1], or w[len(w) - 1]. Using w[len(w)] goes one past the end and crashes.
A different word, to check nothing was typed in by hand instead of being worked out.

tasks.fb: len() counts the characters. Positions run from 0 to len() - 1, so the last one is len() - 1, which is also written as -1.

tasks.q: Write a program that prints the character at a position the user chooses, and says so politely when there is no character there.
brief: Read one word, then read one whole number - a position counting from 0.
If that position exists in the word, print the character at it.
Otherwise print: no such position
tasks.starter: # Read a word and a position, then print the character there if it exists

tests.why: Position 0 is the first character. If you got l, you added 1 to the position somewhere.
planet has 6 characters, so the highest position is 5. Rejecting this means you tested p < len(w) - 1 instead of p < len(w).
Position 6 is one past the end. This is the classic off-by-one: the number of characters is 6, but the last position is 5.
A one-character word still has position 0.
There is no position 1 in a word of one character. Comparing against the length rather than a fixed number is what makes this work for any word.

tasks.fb: A string of length n has positions 0 to n - 1. Check against the length, never against a number you typed in yourself.

tasks.q: Write a program that makes a three-letter code from the start of a word.
brief: Read one word.
If it has 3 or more characters, print its first 3 characters and nothing else.
If it has fewer than 3 characters, print: too short
tasks.starter: # Read a word and print its first three characters, or say it is too short

tests.why: The slice w[0:3] takes positions 0, 1 and 2 - three characters. A harb means you wrote w[0:4], which takes four.
A word of exactly 3 characters gives all three. Getting ca means you wrote w[0:2] and counted the end of a slice as included.
Two characters is fewer than 3. Python would happily give you no for w[0:3] without complaining, so you have to check the length yourself.
One character. If you printed q, your length check used < 2 or a wrong comparison.
A different word, so a program that printed a code it had been told in advance will fail here.

tasks.fb: In a slice w[a:b], a is included and b is not. So w[0:3] is three characters, and the 3 is the position after the last one you want.

tasks.q: A label is wrapped in one marker character at each end. Write a program that prints what is inside the markers.
brief: Read one line of text.
If it has 3 or more characters, print it with the first and the last character removed.
If it has fewer than 3 characters, print: nothing inside
tasks.starter: # Print the line without its first and last characters

tests.why: Start at position 1 and stop before the last position. A tulip# means you took the first character off but left the last one on.
Two characters are left. Getting a means you stopped one too early - try s[1:len(s) - 1], not s[1:len(s) - 2].
Exactly 3 characters leaves one in the middle. An empty line here means your slice ended before the character you wanted.
Two characters means both of them are markers, so there is nothing inside. A slice would quietly return an empty string, which is why the length check is needed.
An empty line has no characters at all. A crash here means you looked at s[0] before checking the length.

tasks.fb: s[1:len(s) - 1] drops one character from each end. Taking a slice off the end of a string never crashes, it just gives you less than you expected, so check the length first.

tasks.q: Write a program that compares two words, treating capitals as the same as small letters, and puts them in order when they differ.
brief: Read two words, one per line.
If they are the same word once capitals are ignored, print: match - and nothing else.
Otherwise print: different - and then on a second line print whichever of the two words comes first in alphabetical order, again ignoring capitals.
Print that word exactly as it was typed.
tasks.starter: # Compare the two words ignoring capitals, and say which comes first if they differ

tests.why: Only the capital H differs. Comparing a == b directly says these are different, because H and h are not the same character to Python.
Both words have to be changed to the same case before comparing. Changing only one of them still leaves them unequal.
An extra s makes them different words, and the shorter one comes first. Ignoring capitals does not mean ignoring letters.
A single letter in either case. This is the smallest possible version of the same test.

Every capital letter has a lower code than every small letter, so comparing the words as typed puts Zebra first. Lower the case of both before comparing them with <, as well as before testing them with ==.

tasks.fb: Put both strings into the same case before comparing - .lower() on both, or .upper() on both. This matters for < just as much as for ==, because A has code 65 and a has code 97.

tasks.q: Write a program that counts how many of the characters in a line are capital letters.
brief: Read one line of text.
Count how many of its characters are capital letters.
Print only that count.
tasks.starter: # Go through the line one character at a time and count the capitals

tests.why: A, L and F are capitals; the rest are not. A 15 here means you counted every character instead of testing each one.
No capitals at all, so the answer is 0. Your counter has to be set to 0 before the loop so it still prints something.
One capital letter on its own.
M, D and C are capitals. The digit 3 and the space are not letters, so they must not be counted - a test like ch < 'a' would wrongly count both.
An empty line has nothing to count. The loop runs zero times and the counter is still 0.

tasks.fb: A character is a capital when it is different from its own lower-case version. Digits and spaces are the same in either case, so this test leaves them out on its own.

tasks.q: Write a program that checks whether one piece of text appears somewhere inside another, and says whether it is right at the start.
brief: Read one line of text, then read the word to look for.
If the word does not appear anywhere in the text, print: missing - and nothing else.
If it does appear, print: found - and then on a second line print: at the start - if the text begins with that word, or: inside - if it does not.
tasks.starter: # Say whether the word is in the text, and whether the text begins with it

tests.why: tide appears in the middle of the text. The in operator looks anywhere, so it tells you the word is there but not where - a slice from position 0 is what answers that.
sand is not there at all, so there should be no second line. A program that always prints found will fail here.
The text begins with the. Comparing text[0:len(word)] with the word is what checks this - text[0:3] only works for words of exactly 3 characters.
The word to look for is longer than the text, so it cannot be inside it. Check you have word in text and not text in word - the order matters.
A single character counts as appearing inside the text, and here it is also the first one.
A space is a character like any other, so e t does appear - at the end of the and the start of tide. Splitting the text into words first would make you miss this.

tasks.fb: word in text asks whether word appears anywhere inside text - the thing being looked for comes first. in cannot tell you where, so a slice from position 0 is needed for the second part.

tasks.q: Write a program that reports the position at which a word starts inside a line of text.
brief: Read one line of text, then read the word to look for.
If the word is in the text, print the position where it starts, counting from 0.
If it is not in the text, print: not found
tasks.starter: # Find where the word starts in the text, or say it is not there

tests.why: copper and the space take up positions 0 to 6, so kettle starts at 7. An 8 means you counted from 1 instead of 0.
A word at the very start is at position 0. A 1 here means you added 1 to make it look more natural - the brief asks for counting from 0.
find() returns -1 when nothing matches. Printing -1 is not what the brief asks for, so you have to test for it and print the words instead.
There are three letter e characters, and find() reports only the first, at position 4. Printing a later one means you kept looking after the first match.
The first place aa fits is right at the start, so the answer is 0 and not 1.

tasks.fb: find() gives the position of the first match, or -1 when there is none. -1 is not a position, so always test for it before you print.

tasks.q: Write a program that prints the letter that comes after the one given, going back to the start of the alphabet after z.
brief: Read one lower-case letter.
If it is z, print: a
Otherwise print the letter that comes next in the alphabet.
Use ord() and chr() to work it out.
tasks.starter: # Turn the letter into its code, add one, turn it back into a letter

tests.why: ord('d') is 100, so the next code is 101, which chr() turns back into e. Forgetting chr() prints the number 101 instead of a letter.
a has code 97, so b has code 98. Taking 1 away instead of adding it would give the letter before.
ord('z') is 122, and 123 is the { character, not a letter. The alphabet has to be wrapped round by hand, which is what the special case for z is for.
y is the last letter that needs no wrapping. Treating y as the special case as well would wrongly skip z.

tasks.fb: ord() turns a character into its code and chr() turns a code back into a character. ord('a') is 97 and ord('z') is 122, so code 123 is past the end of the alphabet.

tasks.q: Write a program that separates the letters and the digits in a line of text.
brief: Read one line of text.
Build up two new strings: one of its letters in the order they appear, one of its digits in the order they appear.
Anything that is neither a letter nor a digit is thrown away.
Print the letters on the first line, or print: none - if there are no letters.
Print the digits on the second line, or print: none - if there are no digits.
tasks.starter: # Build two new strings, one character at a time

tests.why: The letters keep their order and so do the digits. Printing each character as you meet it gives ten lines instead of two - build the strings up first and print them at the end.
No letters at all, so the first line is the word none. An empty first line means you printed the empty string instead of testing for it.
No digits this time. Both the letters string and the digits string need to be set to an empty string before the loop.
One of each. Codes 97 to 122 are the small letters and 48 to 57 are the digits.
Nothing to sort at all, so both lines are none. The loop runs zero times, which is why the two strings must start out empty rather than unset.

tasks.fb: Adding to a string makes a new one: letters = letters + ch. The codes are 65 to 90 for capitals, 97 to 122 for small letters and 48 to 57 for the digits 0 to 9.

tasks.q: Write a program that reverses a word and says whether it reads the same both ways.
brief: Read one word.
Build the word backwards one character at a time - do not use a slice with a negative step and do not use reversed().
Print the reversed word on the first line.
If the word reads the same forwards and backwards once capitals are ignored, print: palindrome - on the second line.
Otherwise print: not a palindrome - on the second line.
tasks.starter: # Build the reversed word one character at a time, then compare

tests.why: Each new character goes in front of what you have so far: rev = ch + rev. Writing rev = rev + ch just copies the word unchanged, which would also wrongly call it a palindrome.
The reversed word keeps the letters where they are, so the capital L moves to the end. The palindrome test has to ignore capitals, or Level would not match leveL.
A single character is its own reverse, so it is always a palindrome. A crash here means your loop used positions that assumed more than one character.
kayak is a palindrome but kayaks is not - the extra s at one end only. This catches a comparison that stopped before the last character.
A palindrome of an even number of characters has no middle letter, so a loop that stopped at the middle would get this wrong.

tasks.fb: Putting each character in front of what you have already built reverses a string. Compare the reversed version with the original in the same case to test for a palindrome.
forbid: The brief asks you to build the reversed word yourself, one character at a time, not with a reversing slice.
The brief asks you to build the reversed word yourself, one character at a time, not with reversed().

stations.name: Final challenge: what does it give?

tasks.q: The word is LANTERN. What does each piece of Python give back?
tasks.fb: Counting from 0, and a slice that stops before its second number, explain most of these.

info.title: Spaces count
info.text: len() counts every character, so a space, a comma and a full stop each add one to the length.

info.title: Open ends
info.text: A slice can leave a number out: word[:3] starts at the beginning and word[3:] runs to the end.

info.title: Nothing is changed
info.text: upper() does not change the original - it hands back a new string. Strings in Python cannot be edited in place.

info.title: Searching fairly
info.text: To search without caring about capitals, lower() both the text and the thing you are looking for before you search.

info.title: Beyond A to Z
info.text: ord() gives a Unicode code point, so it works for letters from any alphabet, not only A to Z.

info.title: Building strings
info.text: Adding to a string makes a brand new one each time. For a long job, collecting the pieces in a list and joining them once is quicker.
